resource.name: Supply Chain Shipment Pricing Dataset
resource.description: This dataset provides supply chain health commodity shipment and pricing data. Specifically, the data set identifies Antiretroviral (ARV) and HIV lab shipments to supported countries. In addition, the data set provides the commodity pricing and associated supply chain expenses necessary to move the commodities to countries for use. The dataset has similar fields to the Global Fund's Price, Quality and Reporting (PQR) data. PEPFAR and the Global Fund represent the two largest procurers of HIV health commodities. This dataset, when analyzed in conjunction with the PQR data, provides a more complete picture of global spending on specific health commodities. The data are particularly valuable for understanding ranges and trends in pricing as well as volumes delivered by country. The US Government believes this data will help stakeholders make better, data-driven decisions. Care should be taken to consider contextual factors when using the database. Conclusions related to costs associated with moving specific line items or products to specific countries and lead times by product/country will not be accurate.

resource.name: USAID Anticorruption Projects Database
resource.description: The Anticorruption Projects Database (Database) includes information about USAID projects with anticorruption interventions implemented worldwide between 2007 and 2013. The Database includes about 300 long-term country projects and regional or short-term projects. Projects were identified and information collected by the six Implementing Partners (IP) of the ENGAGE Indefinite Quantity Contract. Criteria for selecting projects included: distinctive project interventions targeted at reducing corruption or promoting government integrity, accountability and transparency that ultimately results in reducing opportunities to corruption. Availability of sufficient information about the projects was another criterion for selecting them to the Database. This included but was not limited to project description and results, implementation timeframe, project value, and implementer. After reviewing approximately 2000 projects, more than 300 were identified for the Database.

resource.name: Genes Controlling Black Seed Coat and Pod Tip Color in Cowpea: Phenotype Data for the Sanzi by Vita 7 population
resource.description: Seed coat color is an important part of consumer preferences for cowpea (Vigna unguiculata [L.] Walp). Color has been studied in numerous crop species and has often been linked to loci controlling the anthocyanin biosynthesis pathway. This study makes use of available resources, including mapping populations, a reference genome, and a high-density single nucleotide polymorphism genotyping platform, to map the black seed coat and purple pod tip color traits, with the gene symbol Bl, in cowpea. Several gene models encoding MYB domain protein 113 were identified as candidate genes. MYB domain proteins have been shown in other species to control expression of genes encoding enzymes for the final steps in the anthocyanin biosynthesis pathway. PCR analysis indicated that a presence/absence variation of one or more MYB113 genes may control the presence or absence of black pigment. A PCR marker has been developed for the MYB113 gene Vigun05g039500, a candidate gene for black seed coat color in cowpea.

domain_metadata.value: University of California Riverside. 2023. Genes Controlling Black Seed Coat and Pod Tip Color in Cowpea: Phenotype Data for the Sanzi by Vita 7 population. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/jwzr-34nr.
Bureau for Resilience and Food Security

Advances in genomics over the past several years have enabled the elucidation the genetic basis of black seed coat and purple pod tip color, traits first described nearly one hundred years ago. This study maps black seed coat and purple pod tip color in several independently generated populations and provides candidate genes. Using high-throughput SNP genotyping and whole genome sequencing, previously impossible levels of mapping precision have been achieved. The presence of a deletion is supported by PCR evidence and sequence alignment from thirty-seven accessions. The identification of MYB transcription factors as candidate genes is supported by prior literature on homologous genes performing similar functions in other species, including Arabidopsis, grape, citrus, and soybean. The PCR-based markers developed here provide a useful tool for breeders engaged in marker-assisted selection for seed coat color in cowpea.

resource.name: Section G Food Safety Measures
resource.description: The survey interviewed 254 retailer shops in 10 sub-cities of Addis Ababa. 30 supermarkets, 20 mini-markets, 100 regular shops, 80 dairy shops and 24 open market shops selling dairy products were interviewed. Details of the sampling strategy is found in the attachment. The survey collected information on the characteristics of the shop, details of dairy products sold, prices and quality. Policy makers, research, and other stakeholders can use this data to analyses dairy value chain in Ethiopia and dairy retailing practices in Ethiopia. This data set was collected through research of the project “Improving the evidence and policies for better performing livestock systems in Ethiopia” lead by the International Food Policy Research Institution as part of the Feed the Future Innovation Lab for Livestock Systems.

resource.name: Feed the Future Malawi Interim Survey in the Zone of Infuence, Children's File
resource.description: This dataset contains records describing for all children under 5 years of age sampled during the 2015 Feed the Future Malawi Interim Survey in the Zone of Influence.  The survey was designed to monitor program performance by periodic assessments of a number of standardized indicators.  A total of 1,021 households were interviewed, which provided data for the target sample size of 1,007 households and ensured the sample is representative of the seven districts covered in the interim assessment.  This dataset includes data from Module I for children’s anthropometry and infant and young child feeding practices. The anthropometry Z-scores were calculated in SAS during the data management process, using the World Health Organization (WHO) SAS “igrowup” package. The unique identifiers for this file are pbs_id + idcode.

resource.name: Feed the Future-Ethiopia PRIME-Interim Survey-October 2014 through April 2015
resource.description: This dataset is the first of two interim surveys administered from October 2014 through April 2015 to enable the Feed the Future PRIME project in Ethiopia to monitor program performance by reviewing changes in a number of standardized indicators.  These indicators reflect data collected through population-based surveys (PBS) in the geographic areas targeted by Feed the Future interventions, known as the Feed the Future Zones of Influence (ZOI).  Each survey was administered to a sample of over 400 households in 17 kebeles (communities) once a month over a 6-month period creating for a total of six rounds of data for each survey.

resource.name: Crustaceans and Demersal, Large Pelagic and Small Pelagic Fish (Length Data)
resource.description:
Length data provides biological information and attributes of the catches of each sampled vessel that covers: organization/project; ID trip; surveyor; sampling; site sampling time; commodity; WPP; vessel name/owner; fishing gear; catcher; collector; fishing areas; total catch in volume (Kg); total catch in units (Ind); total sampling in volume (Kg); total sampling in units (Ind); sample name; total (Kg); units (Ind); length type; common name; species name; length (Cm).

The Length data is used best to assess the state of the fish stocks for fish species sampled using several modelling approaches such as the LBSPR (Length Based – Spawning Potential Ratio) that is, a relative rate of production in fish stock that have been exploited based on fish length. Other than that, this data also can provide 1) growth estimation parameter 2) Mortality 3) Fishing gear selectivity 4) recruitment pattern and 5) estimated fish mortality due to natural factors.

resource.name: Genes Controlling Black Seed Coat and Pod Tip Color in Cowpea: Output Data for the CB27 by IT82E-18 population
resource.description: Seed coat color is an important part of consumer preferences for cowpea (Vigna unguiculata [L.] Walp). Color has been studied in numerous crop species and has often been linked to loci controlling the anthocyanin biosynthesis pathway. This study makes use of available resources, including mapping populations, a reference genome, and a high-density single nucleotide polymorphism genotyping platform, to map the black seed coat and purple pod tip color traits, with the gene symbol Bl, in cowpea. Several gene models encoding MYB domain protein 113 were identified as candidate genes. MYB domain proteins have been shown in other species to control expression of genes encoding enzymes for the final steps in the anthocyanin biosynthesis pathway. PCR analysis indicated that a presence/absence variation of one or more MYB113 genes may control the presence or absence of black pigment. A PCR marker has been developed for the MYB113 gene Vigun05g039500, a candidate gene for black seed coat color in cowpea.

domain_metadata.value: University of California Riverside. 2023. Genes Controlling Black Seed Coat and Pod Tip Color in Cowpea: Output Data for the CB27 by IT82E-18 population. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/k4vq-rk23.
Bureau for Resilience and Food Security

Advances in genomics over the past several years have enabled the elucidation the genetic basis of black seed coat and purple pod tip color, traits first described nearly one hundred years ago. This study maps black seed coat and purple pod tip color in several independently generated populations and provides candidate genes. Using high-throughput SNP genotyping and whole genome sequencing, previously impossible levels of mapping precision have been achieved. The presence of a deletion is supported by PCR evidence and sequence alignment from thirty-seven accessions. The identification of MYB transcription factors as candidate genes is supported by prior literature on homologous genes performing similar functions in other species, including Arabidopsis, grape, citrus, and soybean. The PCR-based markers developed here provide a useful tool for breeders engaged in marker-assisted selection for seed coat color in cowpea.

resource.name: Nepal Business Literacy Impact Evaluation - Baseline Household Dataset
resource.description:
Feed the Future activities in Nepal include the Business Literacy (BL) Program, which operates in conjunction with the Knowledge-Based Integrated Sustainable Agriculture and Nutrition (KISAN) Project. Nepal Business Literacy (BL) Impact Evaluation (IE) is designed to collect and analyze three rounds of qualitative and quantitative data collected in order to learn from evidence of the extent to which initial and persistent results of the BL training course occur. The Nepal BL IE is designed to investigate initial and longer-term or persistent impacts of the training experience on targeted aspects of beneficiaries’ knowledge, skills, attitudes (KSA), and behaviors. Investigators also are interested in whether and to what extent the BL training experience leads to adoption of targeted behaviors, such as starting new micro enterprises, that persist over time. resource.name: Telephonic Survey of Domestic Election Observers Trained Under Citizen Voice Project (CVP): Dataset
resource.description: In response to challenges identified in Pakistan’s 2013 national elections, the United States Agency for International Development in Pakistan (USAID/Pakistan) designed the Pakistan Electoral and Democratic Support (PEDS) project to increase citizen confidence in the civilian government and strengthen the environment for free and fair elections. The project employed an integrated approach to strengthen linkages between the Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP), local civil society organizations, and political parties. The project consisted of four components: the Strengthening Electoral and Legislative Processes (SELP) program, implemented by the United Nations Development Program (UNDP); the Political Party Development Program (PPDP), implemented by the National Democratic Institute (NDI); the Prevention of Election-related Violence, implemented by the United States Institute of Peace (USIP). The program review assessed the effectiveness of each of the PEDS components; and the Citizens’ Voice Project (CVP), implemented by the Trust for Democratic Education and Accountability (TDEA) and Free and Fair Election Network (FAFEN).

domain_metadata.value: Management Systems International (MSI). 2021. Telephonic Survey of Domestic Election Observers Trained Under Citizen Voice Project (CVP): Dataset. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/k5ya-p2kd.

As a part of the Citizens’ Voice Project (CVP), FAFEN trained domestic elections observers through a cascade training program implemented by six partner organizations in the formerly Federally Administrated Tribal Areas (FATA). The survey team conducted a telephonic survey of domestic observers to assess the understanding of their duties and the extent to which they were able to perform these duties on election day in the newly merged districts of the Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA).  Due to limited access to and large geographic spread of intervention districts, the survey team elected to conduct this survey telephonically. Telephone surveys have inherent limitations. First, the enumerator cannot gauge the body language of the respondent or easily develop a rapport. Second, the telephone survey may underrepresent the views of respondents in regions with poor telephone coverage. Third, the survey team anticipated a high non-response rate. To account for high non-response rates, the survey team increased the minimum required sample sizes for male and female trainers. The achieved sample sizes produced generalizable results within acceptable error limits (four percent absolute margin of error and 95 percent level of confidence for men; seven percent absolute margin of error and 95 percent level of confidence for women).

All unique individual identifiers, including names, addresses, and phone numbers of respondents, as well as names of data collection and processing teams, have been removed from the CVP survey dataset and omitted from the final report. A unique identification code was assigned to each survey respondent, reflecting respondents’ sex, training provider, and district. While these are important variables to explain variation in responses, together they do not provide sufficient information to identify individual respondents.

As a part of the Citizens’ Voice Project (CVP), FAFEN trained domestic elections observers through a cascade training program implemented by six partner organizations in the formerly Federally Administrated Tribal Areas (FATA). In September/October 2019, MSI conducted a telephonic survey of domestic observers of the former Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA), now referred to as the newly merged districts (NMDs) of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) province, to assess their understanding of their duties and the extent to which they were able to perform these duties on election day. The survey provides a quick snapshot of the effectiveness of capacity building efforts for elections observation in remote and difficult-to-access areas of the NMDs. The target population of the survey was 857 (773 male and 84 female) domestic observers trained by FAFEN through a cascade training. The minimum sample sizes required to produce representative results separately generalizable for male and female observers with four percent absolute margin of error and 95 percent level of confidence were 257 men and 68 women, respectively. In anticipation of high non-response rate in a telephonic survey format, the survey team increased its minimum required sample sizes for male and female observers to 589 and 84, respectively. From 773 male observers, the team selected 589 men using simple random sampling, and contacted all 84 women. The enumeration team successfully conducted 437 interviews, including 371 men and 66 women. The achieved sample sizes produced generalizable results within acceptable error limits (four percent absolute margin of error and 95 percent level of confidence for men; seven percent absolute margin of error and 95 percent level of confidence for women).The survey dataset provides respondent data relating to materials received during the training, satisfaction with and perceived utility of the training, knowledge of elections observation practices, and election day experiences (including access to polling stations, number of polling stations observed, permissions to partake in the vote counting process, violence or threats of violence received in the performance of one’s duties, and ability to upload observation data to the FAFEN data portal).In addition to the survey data, no other primary data was collected to inform the team’s analysis.

resource.name: Macedonia Public Opinion Survey (June 2015)
resource.description:
The survey of Macedonian public opinion was conducted on behalf of the International Republican Institute by the Brima market research firm.

Data was collected from June 6 to 15, 2015 using in-person, face-to-face methodology by trained professional interviewers.

A total of 1,105 interviews was completed yielding an overall margin of error of plus or minus three percent at the mid-range of the 95-percent confidence level. A nationally representative sample was based on a multistage stratification proportionate to population sample distribution, with a random selection of households and respondents.

resource.name: Saving Lives at Birth DR Congo NeoBeat Study 2017: Liveborn App Dataset
resource.description:
The Newborn Heart Rate as a Catalyst for Improved Survival (NeoBeat Study) enrolled participants born between 1/1/17 and 06/22/20, with observational data collection beginning October 25, 2018. The primary purpose of this study was to evaluate the effect of resuscitation training and continuous electronic heart rate monitoring on total stillbirths. Three health facilities in Kinshasa, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, participated in the study. 

This dataset includes the observational data collected via an electronic tablet application, “Liveborn”, to document delivery room resuscitations.

domain_metadata.value: Jacquelyn Patterson, Daniel Ishoso, Daniel Ishoso, Joar Eilevstjønn, Melissa Bauserman, Ingunn Haug, Pooja Iyer, Beena D. Kamath-Rayne, Adrien Lokangaka, Casey Lowman, Eric Mafuta, Helge Myklebust, Tracy Nolen, Janna Patterson, Antoinette Tshefu, Carl Bose, Sara K. Berkelhamer

In 2015, approximately 2.6 million pregnancies reportedly ended in stillbirths; 98% occurred in low and lower-middle income countries (LMICs). Nearly one-half of stillbirths were classified as fresh stillbirths, indicating that the fetus died during the intrapartum period. Typically, the diagnosis of a stillbirth was made because the newborn did not breathe following birth. Yet many of these non-breathing newborns classified as stillborn have a heart rate (HR) and are actually live born. The effect of a low-cost monitor for measuring HR on newborn survival is unknown. Knowledge of HR during newborn resuscitation might also result in administration of appropriate interventions, and improvement in outcomes. Helping Babies Breathe (HBB), a resuscitation algorithm developed by the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), is widely accepted as the standard of care for newborn resuscitation in LMICs. In keeping with ILCOR recommendations that HR be measured during newborn resuscitation, HBB calls for heart rate assessment after 1 minute of positive-pressure ventilation with good chest movement (or sooner if there is a helper who can palpate/auscultate HR). However, given the frequent reality of a single provider attending deliveries in LMICs, as well as the currently available methods for assessing HR (i.e. palpation or auscultation), assessment of HR is challenging to perform without delaying or stopping the provision of other life-saving interventions such as bag and mask ventilation.  Furthermore, the most accurate method of HR assessment at birth is an electrocardiogram, which is not widely available in LMICs. NeoBeat is a low-cost alternative to continuously monitor HR that can guide resuscitation in these settings.

The data and metadata that comprise this open access, peer-reviewed technical publication provide insight into the composition and architecture of the genome of cowpea via a high-quality, annotated genome sequence. The annotations include genes, repetitive sequences and positions of nearly one million genetic variants that exist within cultivated cowpeas. Relationships of the cowpea genome to common bean is highlighted, and each cowpea chromosome is mathematically described as recombination rate as a function of nucleotide position. This information provides a framework upon which to hang all past and future information about genetic variation within the species, as well as suites of genetic markers for any trait that has been or will be genetically mapped. Such information is useful for marker-assisted breeding, and to spawn basic research on mechanisms underlying the range of traits of cowpea.

resource.name: Genes Controlling Black Seed Coat and Pod Tip Color in Cowpea: Primer information used for determining the size of the deletion and as the PCR marker
resource.description: Seed coat color is an important part of consumer preferences for cowpea (Vigna unguiculata [L.] Walp). Color has been studied in numerous crop species and has often been linked to loci controlling the anthocyanin biosynthesis pathway. This study makes use of available resources, including mapping populations, a reference genome, and a high-density single nucleotide polymorphism genotyping platform, to map the black seed coat and purple pod tip color traits, with the gene symbol Bl, in cowpea. Several gene models encoding MYB domain protein 113 were identified as candidate genes. MYB domain proteins have been shown in other species to control expression of genes encoding enzymes for the final steps in the anthocyanin biosynthesis pathway. PCR analysis indicated that a presence/absence variation of one or more MYB113 genes may control the presence or absence of black pigment. A PCR marker has been developed for the MYB113 gene Vigun05g039500, a candidate gene for black seed coat color in cowpea.

domain_metadata.value: University of California Riverside. 2023. Genes Controlling Black Seed Coat and Pod Tip Color in Cowpea: Primer information used for determining the size of the deletion and as the PCR marker. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/khcc-vzez.
Bureau for Resilience and Food Security

Advances in genomics over the past several years have enabled the elucidation the genetic basis of black seed coat and purple pod tip color, traits first described nearly one hundred years ago. This study maps black seed coat and purple pod tip color in several independently generated populations and provides candidate genes. Using high-throughput SNP genotyping and whole genome sequencing, previously impossible levels of mapping precision have been achieved. The presence of a deletion is supported by PCR evidence and sequence alignment from thirty-seven accessions. The identification of MYB transcription factors as candidate genes is supported by prior literature on homologous genes performing similar functions in other species, including Arabidopsis, grape, citrus, and soybean. The PCR-based markers developed here provide a useful tool for breeders engaged in marker-assisted selection for seed coat color in cowpea.

resource.name: Feed the Future Senegal: Yaajeende Production Data
resource.description:
The purpose of this study is to evaluate the impact that the Feed the Future Nutrition-led Agriculture Project for Food Security in Senegal (known as "Yaajeende") has had on reducing malnutrition and poverty in its intervention area.

This report details the findings, conclusions and recommendations of a mixed-methods quasi-experimental final impact evaluation (FIE) of the United States Agency for International Development’s (USAID) $50 million, seven-year Feed the Future Nutrition-Led Agriculture Project for Food Security in Senegal, known as “Yaajeende.” The National Cooperative Business Association’s Cooperative League of the USA (NCBA CLUSA) implemented the project. To combat poverty and child malnutrition, Yaajeende sought to accelerate the participation of the very poor in rural economic growth and improve the four dimensions of food security: availability, access, utilization and stability. Yaajeende worked in 790 villages across 49 municipalities (“communes” in French) and nine departments in the Matam, Tambacounda, Kédougou and Kolda regions. The project’s implementation period was November 1, 2010, to September 30, 2017.

The FIE aims to provide USAID with an evidence base on the impacts of the nutrition-led agriculture (NLA) approach that the project utilized on its key objectives, including reduced poverty and malnutrition. The findings are expected to provide accountability and learning value to USAID, including both the Senegal Mission and USAID/Feed the Future. Additional stakeholders include the Government of Senegal, implementing partners and other agencies, donors and practitioners active in nutrition, health, agriculture and integrated sectors.

resource.name: FtF Kenya Household Survey 2015: Livestock Data
resource.description:
The dataset file can be found in the metadata below.

The Kenya Agricultural Value Chain Enterprises (KAVES) activity works with smallholder farmers, businesses, and national and county government partners to address constraints up and down the value chain (such as agro-processors, input suppliers, transporters, exporters, retailers, financiers) and develop fully-functioning, competitive value chains. KAVES aims to increase the productivity and incomes of smallholder farmers, and other actors along the value chain, who are working in the dairy, maize (and other staples), and horticulture sectors.

This data is derived from a 2015 survey collecting year-end results on activities related to crop production and sales, livestock production and sales, nutrition, water and sanitation, and access to financial services. Respondents are beneficiaries of the Kenya-­KAVES project.

domain_metadata.value: Fintrac, Inc.. 2020. FtF Kenya Household Survey 2015: Livestock Data. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/kvib-e447.

We identified variables within the asset that present privacy risk (key variables) and applied a 3-anonymity technique on categorical key variables, such as county, sex and age group. In order to reach the 3-anonymity threshold, we recoded some variables and suppressed values that increased the risk of re-identification. Doing so reduces the precision of the cells, while preserving statistical utility. 3-anonymity mitigates risk on key categorical variables in a combined way.
Data were collected for a wide range of variables to better inform the design of the project and could potentially be reused to plan additional projects in the same sectors in other regions.

resource.name: Survey data for weed seedbank across farms with varying tillage practices in Eastern India
resource.description: This project compiled germinable seedbank counts from 84 farmers’ fields in Bihar and Eastern Uttar Pradesh, India. Soil samples were submitted for soil texture and chemical analyses. Seedbank soil samples were collected from pairs of neighboring fields with similar soils and microclimates but differing in historic tillage (conventional tillage [CT] versus zero tillage [ZT]) and crop rotation practices (rice­-wheat versus rice­maize/potato-­rice­-wheat).
resource.attribution: US Borlaug Fellows in Global Food Security

domain_metadata.value: Carolyn Lowry. 2020. Survey data for weed seedbank across farms with varying tillage practices in Eastern India. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/m7vb-rcbw.
Time required for manuscript preparation after data submission.

Soil samples for weed seedbank analysis were collected from pairs of neighboring fields with similar soils and microclimates but differing in tillage and crop rotation practices, across three regions in Bihar and Eastern Uttar Pradesh: Samastipur-Vaishali-Muzaffarpur (SVM), Ara-Buxar (AB) and Maharajgunj-Kushinagar (MK). In total we collected soil from 84 farmer fields. Soil samples were collected to a depth of 15 cm from each field following rice harvest but before wheat planting. Soil cores from each fieldwere composited and air dried until the germination assay. We utilized 2 subsamples of 500 ml of soil each from each farm for seedbank analysis. Soils were brought to a common greenhouse, spread in a thin layer in flats, and evaluated for germinable seedbank through exhaustive germination; soil subsamples were analysed for soil texture, and soil chemical characteristics including pH, electrical conductivity (EC), organic carbon (OC), P, K, Mg and Ca.

All survey specific data elements should be removed as they are only useful in managing the implementation of the survey: date of interview, ability to be interviewed alone, outcome of the interview.

A range of household level data elements were reported in all other datasets and should be removed from all datasets except household’s. Examples include dwelling characteristics (roof, floor, walls) and hunger scale questions.

We will use the following steps to anonymize the datasets:
1.	Use k-anonymity to mitigate the following variables: sex, dwelling characteristics, relationship to household head, type of toilets, education level, literacy level (read and write), district, urbanization. To achieve a threshold of k=3, we will recode some of these variables including dwelling characteristics, type of toilets, relationship to household head, education level, and literacy level  
2.	Aggregate age variable into 5 ages bands. 
3.	Apply a micro aggregation to children and women weights and heights. Micro Aggregation replaces each single value with local means calculated on batches of 3 records each. 
4.	Top code the age and estimated price of house. Any reported house age value above 100 years was recoded as 100; any estimated price at 5 000 000 or above was replaced with the mean price of houses costing 5 000 000 or more. 
5.	      5. Capping household size to 13. To achieve this, we will randomly select out of the datasets individual members from these large households who do not participate anywhere else in the survey other than their membership to household. Initially, the largest household had 21 members; after this process, this household would have 13 members. The median household in Kenya is about 4.4. In this data, the median remains at 5.0 before and after households disclosure risk mitigation.

resource.name: Ethiopia Land Governance Activity Baseline Survey 2021: Dataset
resource.description: This dataset, containing 171 rows and 150 columns, presents the results of the quantitative baseline study conducted in the pilot urban and peri-urban areas of Dukem Town, from January 20, 2021 to February 20, 2021, to establish baseline data for comparison to support the program impact measurement as part of future project evaluation and to guide a realistic and feasible target setting for the selected performance indicators. A household survey was administered to a representative sample of 171 households (out of the 1,500 targeted households) in Dukem town to collect quantitative data with a questionnaire length of an average of 50 minutes. All personally identifiable information (e.g., GIS data) was removed from the dataset to protect the personal information of survey respondents. The Feed the Future Ethiopia Land Governance Activity (LGA) is a five-year project funded by USAID, following three successfully implemented land governance projects it supported during 2005 – 2018, i.e. (i) Ethiopia Land Tenure Administration Project (ELTAP) 2005- 2008; Ethiopia Land Administration Project (ELAP) 2008-2013, and Land Administration to Nurture Development (LAND) 2013-2018.

This baseline data will be compared with the end line survey data, which will be collected in 2024 to define the project's impact over time. USAID will use these findings to review the program performance and apply the lessons learned and good practices for the design of follow-up or similar interventions.

resource.name: Baseline Study of Food for Peace Title II Development Food Assistance Program in Karamoja, Uganda--Child Health
resource.description: This dataset describes the children and their health interviewed as part of Baseline Study of Food for Peace Title II Development Food Assistance Program in Karamoja, Uganda.  This dataset contains data from Module D of the questionnaire and has 201 columns and 6,001 rows.  In fiscal year 2012, USAID's Office of Food for Peace (FFP) awarded funding to private voluntary organizations (PVOs) to design and implement a multi-year Title II development food assistance program in Uganda.  The main purpose of the Title II program is to improve long-term food security of chronically food insecure population in the target regions.  FFP contracted a firm, ICF International to conduct a baseline study in targeted areas of the country prior to the start of the new program.  The purpose of the study was to assess the current status of key indicators, have a better understanding of prevailing conditions and perceptions of the population in the implementation areas, and serve as a point of comparison for future final evaluations.  Results would also be used to further refine program targeting and, where possible, to understand the relationship between variables to inform program design.  The study was conducted in 2013, while FFP expects to conduct final evaluations as close as possible to the end of the program five years later.  The data asset is comprised of six datasets: 1) a description of all members of the households surveyed, 2) data on maternal health and sanitation practices, 3) data about the children in the household, 4) data describing the agricultural practices of the household, 5) data describing the food consumption of the household (broken into 4 smaller spreadsheets), and 6) and a description of the weights that should be applied during the analysis of the other datasets.

resource.name: Genes Controlling Black Seed Coat and Pod Tip Color in Cowpea: Allele effects of significant SNPs showing the highest association with black seed coat and purple pod tip color in the minicore population
resource.description: Seed coat color is an important part of consumer preferences for cowpea (Vigna unguiculata [L.] Walp). Color has been studied in numerous crop species and has often been linked to loci controlling the anthocyanin biosynthesis pathway. This study makes use of available resources, including mapping populations, a reference genome, and a high-density single nucleotide polymorphism genotyping platform, to map the black seed coat and purple pod tip color traits, with the gene symbol Bl, in cowpea. Several gene models encoding MYB domain protein 113 were identified as candidate genes. MYB domain proteins have been shown in other species to control expression of genes encoding enzymes for the final steps in the anthocyanin biosynthesis pathway. PCR analysis indicated that a presence/absence variation of one or more MYB113 genes may control the presence or absence of black pigment. A PCR marker has been developed for the MYB113 gene Vigun05g039500, a candidate gene for black seed coat color in cowpea.

domain_metadata.value: University of California Riverside. 2023. Genes Controlling Black Seed Coat and Pod Tip Color in Cowpea: Allele effects of significant SNPs showing the highest association with black seed coat and purple pod tip color in the minicore population. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/mr86-xkg5.
Bureau for Resilience and Food Security

Advances in genomics over the past several years have enabled the elucidation the genetic basis of black seed coat and purple pod tip color, traits first described nearly one hundred years ago. This study maps black seed coat and purple pod tip color in several independently generated populations and provides candidate genes. Using high-throughput SNP genotyping and whole genome sequencing, previously impossible levels of mapping precision have been achieved. The presence of a deletion is supported by PCR evidence and sequence alignment from thirty-seven accessions. The identification of MYB transcription factors as candidate genes is supported by prior literature on homologous genes performing similar functions in other species, including Arabidopsis, grape, citrus, and soybean. The PCR-based markers developed here provide a useful tool for breeders engaged in marker-assisted selection for seed coat color in cowpea.

resource.name: Feed The Future Interim Population-Based Assessment of Cambodia, Module E1-08, Food Shared With Others During the Last Week
resource.description: This dataset captures information about food shared with others during the 7 days before the survey from the first interim assessment of Feed the Future's population-based indicaors for the ZOI in Cambodia.  It has 1019 rows and 14 columns.  The ZOI is the Pursat, Battambang, Kampong Thom, and Siem Reap Provinces.  The sampling design called for a two-stage cluster sample.  In the first stage, 84 villages were selected; in the second stage, households were selected within each sampled village. The sampling of villages was stratified by province, with the number of villages in each stratum proportional to the population in the stratum and with villages selected with probability proportional to size, based on the 2013 Commune Database.  The data is split into survey modules.  Modules A through C includes location information, informed consent, and the household roster.  Module D includes household characteristics.  Module E is the expenditures module broken up into 8 different parts.  Modules F and G include the hunger scale data and WEIA index data.  Data in modules H and I include mother and child dietary diversity.

resource.name: West Usambara Plateau Sites
resource.description:
In this manuscript, we synthesize current and legacy data from multiple studies to better understand the distribution and diversity of soil types and their properties in the Plateau physiographic region of the West Usamabara Mountains in Northeastern Tanzania. Analysis of soil properties and soil classification in the resulting dataset of 468 sites by land use, landscape position, and elevation revealed important relationships relevant for management and land use planning. These sites occurred across a range of landscape positions and an elevation gradient from 1040 – 2240 m.a.s.l. Soil diversity at the U.S. Order and WRB Reference Group levels was higher than expected, with five U.S. soil orders and seven WRB Reference Groups described in the dataset, and the highest soil diversity occurring at lower landscape positions. We found that soil organic carbon (SOC) and pH were two master variables that were correlated most other soil properties. Sites under cultivated land uses had the lowest topsoil soil organic carbon (SOC) concentrations, and SOC generally increased with increasing elevation. Mature forest and charcoal production areas did not significantly differ in their depth distributions of SOC. Valley soils had significantly lower surface SOC concentrations but higher exchangeable bases and pH values than all other landscape positions. Soil pH decreased by an average of 3.5 units across the entire elevation gradient and decreased by 1 unit with elevation even after SOC, land use and landscape position were included in multiple regression models. Local pedotransfer functions were developed to assist with the use of pH, clay and SOC as proxies for more difficult to measure soil properties such as cation exchange capacity (CEC) and base saturation (B.S.), bulk density and total phosphorus. Phosphorus (P) and potassium (K) were
identified as the most likely limiting nutrients in West Usambaran plateau soils in general. This information is critical for sustainable land management which will be applicable to the soils of other mountain complexes in the Eastern Arc chain.

resource.description: The Comprehensive African Agriculture Development Program (CAADP) was designed to promote interventions that best respond to the recognized precarious situation of African agriculture. Its focused goals are (a) extending the area under sustainable land management and reliable water control systems; (b) improving rural infrastructure and trade-related capacities for improved market access; and (c) increasing food supply and reducing hunger. The CAADP also pays attention to emergencies and disasters that require food and agricultural responses or safety nets.

resource.name: Agricultural Land Dynamics and Land Policy in Rural Tanzania 2016: Seed Cost Dataset
resource.description:
This dataset contains information about expenditures on seed. The table can be combined with other datasets in this data asset using the 'hhid' column.

The purpose of collecting these data was to examine farm expansion and labor markets in rural Tanzania. Data were collected in 8 rural districts of Tanzania: Mvomero, Kilombero, Njombe, Kiteto, Magu, Moshi Rural, Mkuranga and Liwale.

The data were collected through the Feed the Future Innovation Lab for Food Security Policy (FSP).

domain_metadata.value: Margaret Beaver. 2019. Agricultural Land Dynamics and Land Policy in Rural Tanzania 2016: Seed Cost Dataset. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/n2sw-zmzg.
See the word document "2016_ALDSDataFileNotes.doc" for details on specific variables that may have data issues. Some plot areas were not allocated by crop but given as total area (see notes)

value: Full dates with month/day/year (Includes: birth, marriage, divorce, hire dates, etc.)

domain_metadata.value:
Examine the rate of land expansion of medium- and large-scale farms compared
to small scale farms, look at policy implications of consequent changes in
farm structure and the concentration of food production and marketed output;
Examine the pace of acquisition of agricultural land by medium- and
large-scale investors through de facto land administration policies; examine
the implication of such dynamics on rural youth land accessibility and out
migration in the context of customary tenure systems; assess the broader
effects of changing farm structure on the types of pace of non-farm
employment growth; understand the relationship between farm size and
efficiency, including the range of factors and policies that might condition
this relationship and specifically examine the impacts of large commercial
agricultural operations on the welfare of rural communities around them.
Examine the extent of land disputes and conflicts in rural Tanzania, their
causes, possible resolution mechanisms, and policy implications to land
investments in Tanzania as well as the implications of the formal and
informal land tenure systems in shaping incidence and intensity of land
dynamics.

resource.name: Farm Plots Survey for Agriculture for Children's Empowerment (ACE) in Liberia- Fertilizer and Seed Endline Dataset
resource.description:
The STRIVE project, funded by USAID's Displaced Children and Orphans Fund (DCOF) and managed by FHI 360, used market-led economic strengthening initiatives to improve the well-being of vulnerable children. Through STRIVE, ACDI/VOCA implemented the Agriculture for Children’s Empowerment (ACE) Project in Liberia, which is founded on the premise that increased household economic security will stimulate more consistent investments in children’s well being via longer term social investments in education and nutrition. ACE’s primary focus was on the horticulture value chain (VC) — the production and marketing of vegetables by smallholder farmers in Montserrado, Bong, and Nimba counties of Liberia. ACE also strengthened smallholder rice farming to increase household food security using a market-sensitive approach to rice seed lending and cultivation.
 
This dataset contains endline information about the fertilizer and seed used on each plot the household owns.

We have used the following steps to anonymize the datasets:1. Remove location variables such as county and Village and retain District 2. Use k-anonymity to mitigate the following variables sex, occupation, relationship to household head, education, dwelling characteristics, and District. To achieve the threshold of k=3, we will recode variables occupation, relationship to household head, education, dwelling characteristics, and District into broader categories 3. Aggregate or recode variables such as Age (into 10 years categories), diploma (any diploma above high school into other), and grade (into Primary, Junior High, and Senior High)4. Top code variables such as household size (15+ at baseline and 17+ at Endline) and rent paid. 5. Remove direct identifiers (names and cell phone numbers); remove probing variables such as Other-specify when they contain individuals’ names or reference to individuals with a status of refugee.

This data asset contains information about each plot the household owns, their size, the crops grown on them and the methods used to grow plants on those plots. Baseline and endline surveys were conducted in 2011 and 2013, respectively. Each survey generated 6 datasets including a household dataset, a members’ dataset, and other datasets related to Farm, Fertilization, Harvest, and Workforce.

resource.name: Feed The Future Interim Population-Based Assessment of Cambodia, Modules A through C, Houshold Identification, Roster, and Demographics
resource.description: This dataset captures data describing the members of each household from the first interim assessment of Feed the Future’s population-based indicators for the ZOI in Cambodia.  The ZOI is the Pursat, Battambang, Kampong Thom, and Siem Reap Provinces.  The sampling design called for a two-stage cluster sample.  In the first stage, 84 villages were selected; in the second stage, households were selected within each sampled village. The sampling of villages was stratified by province, with the number of villages in each stratum proportional to the population in the stratum and with villages selected with probability proportional to size, based on the 2013 Commune Database.  The data is split into survey modules.  Modules A through C includes location information, informed consent, and the household roster.  Module D includes household characteristics.  Module E is the expenditures module broken up into 8 different parts.  Modules F and G include the hunger scale data and WEIA index data.  Data in modules H and I include mother and child dietary diversity.

resource.name: Program Evaluation of USAID/Uganda SUSTAIN Activity: Lab Staff Data
resource.description:
USAID/Uganda’s Strengthening Uganda’s Systems for Treating AIDS Nationally (SUSTAIN) activity supports Uganda’s Ministry of Health (MOH) to strengthen quality and comprehensive HIV/AIDS care, prevention, laboratory and tuberculosis (TB) services at selected regional referral and district health care facilities in Uganda, as well as build the capacity of the public health system to sustain these services. SUSTAIN is a six­-year USAID­-funded activity launched in 2010 and implemented by University Research Co., LLC (URC). SUSTAIN is one of many PEPFAR-­funded activities to address the HIV/AIDS epidemic in Uganda. The main objective of the SUSTAIN program evaluation was to examine the activity’s methodology for achieving its
objectives in order to inform future USAID design work. USAID noted that URC had performed well on SUSTAIN, as evidenced by its activity reports, but wanted an evaluation of the approach used by SUSTAIN to inform future program designs. SUSTAIN implementation adapted to contextual changes in the Government of Uganda's (GoU) HIV/AIDS strategy responding to a spike in new infections and people living with HIV, and major shifts in PEPFAR policy.

resource.name: Community Resilience Activity (CRA) Safe Charity Assessment: Phase 1 Exhibit Data
resource.description:
The United States Agency for International Development (USAID)/Pakistan-funded Safe Charity campaign seeks to reduce financial support to violent extremist groups by educating those who give charity about how to direct their charity to safe recipients in Multan and Karachi. In Multan, the campaign trained influential farmers to disseminate safe charity messages to other farmers; and chambers of commerce and industry, trade and marketing associations, and the Rotary Club to reach the business community. In Karachi, the campaign engaged community youth centers to disseminate messages. The campaign timed its activities to align with common periods of charitable giving, namely Ramazan, Eid ul-Fitr, and Eid ul-Azha. 

These surveys established a baseline of current knowledge and practices with respect to safe charity in Multan and Karachi during each giving period and identified changes in knowledge and practices that could be plausibly linked to the safe charity campaign.

domain_tags: institute of social and policy sciences

domain_metadata.value: Management Systems International (MSI). 2020. Community Resilience Activity (CRA) Safe Charity Assessment: Phase 1 Exhibit Data. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/n7sv-crqs.

The assessment conducted structured surveys of farmer and business communities in Multan and of participants of community youth center activities in Karachi. The assessment team collected survey data in two phases, each phase aligning with one of two selected periods of charitable and corresponding safe charity activities. Phase I aligned with activities relating to charitable giving during Ramazan and Eid ul-Fitr and collected data on decision-making patterns, knowledge, attitudes, and behavior with respect to the giving of zakat and fitrana during that period. Phase II aligned with activities relating to charitable giving during Eid ul-Azha and collected data on similar topics with respect to the giving of animal hides. The Phase II sample consisted primarily of individuals who had also participated in the Phase I survey. The primary limitation to the data from the Phase I survey was a snowball sampling approach to identifying survey respondents who had been exposed to safe charity messaging. For example, the survey team relied on farmer leaders, who had directly engaged with the safe charity campaign, to identify other members of farmer communities with knowledge of safe charity activities. While it was necessary to include “secondary” farmers in the survey sample to assess the reach of safe charity messaging within target communities, the survey team could not guarantee that secondary farmers had participated in safe charity activities or been exposed to safe charity messaging. Furthermore, there is a high likelihood of a selection bias in farmer leader referrals. To control for this bias, the survey team identified enough secondary farmers to create a secondary sampling frame, from which respondents could be randomly selected. The primary limitation to the survey of members of the business community was lack of familiarity with the safe charity campaign, particularly among corporate businesses. This may have been due to challenges identifying knowledgeable individuals within corporate businesses, lower levels of engagement between corporate businesses and their respective chambers of commerce, or characteristics of the corporate engagement strategy of the safe charity campaign.  Whereas the Phase I surveys focused on the giving of zakat and fitrana, the Phase II survey focused specifically on safe charity practices for the giving of qurbani. Phase II included only farmers and excluded the business community and Karachi youth center participants. The survey team employed a longitudinal design, surveying the same farmers who participated in Phase I. By surveying the same respondents, the assessment team examined layered (or repeated) exposure to safe charity activities and compared perceptions around different types of giving. However, given the unique circumstances and distinct forms of charity common to each charitable giving period, differences in behavior between Phase I and II should not be construed as change in behavior attributable to the safe charity campaign.

All unique individual identifiers, including names, addresses, and phone numbers of respondents, as well as names of data collection and processing teams, have been removed from the CRA Safe Charity study dataset and omitted from the final report. A unique identification code has been assigned to each survey respondent, reflecting the respondent’s geographic location (city), type of respondent (direct/indirect, farmers/businessman/workshop participants) and sex. The dataset does include information pertaining to respondents’ sex, educational attainment, religion, employment status, and income, which are important variables to explain variation in responses. These variables, however, together do not provide sufficient information to identify individual respondents.

The assessment team, led by MSI and the Institute of Social and Policy Sciences (I-SAPS), conducted structured surveys of farmer and business communities in Multan and of participants of community youth center activities in Karachi. The assessment team collected survey data in two phases, each phase aligning with one of two selected periods of charitable and corresponding safe charity activities. Phase I, which took place in August 2018, aligned with activities relating to charitable giving during Ramazan and Eid ul-Fitr and collected data on decision-making patterns, knowledge, attitudes, and behavior with respect to the giving of zakat and fitrana during that period. Phase II, which took place in October 2018, aligned with activities relating to charitable giving during Eid ul-Azha and collected data on similar topics with respect to the giving of animal hides. The Phase II sample consisted primarily of individuals who had also participated in the Phase I survey. Phase I included three surveys, each targeting a unique respondent group. In Multan, the assessment team selected a random sample of 124 farmer “leaders” from 500 farmers in 11 union councils who were directly engaged by the safe charity campaign. Farmer leaders were pre-identified influential members of their communities, tasked with disseminating information to other farmers and community members through community gatherings, sensitization sessions, and other activities and events. The sample of farmer leaders was stratified by gender and union council. With assistance from farmer leaders, the assessment team then used a snowball approach to identify a sampling frame of at least 500 “secondary” farmers, or members of target communities who participated in community gatherings, sensitizations sessions, and other activities and events sponsored by the safe charity campaign. Using this sampling frame, the assessment team selected a random sample of 150 secondary farmers, also stratified by gender and union council. The assessment team conducted a second Phase I survey of members of chambers of commerce and industry in Multan. The team randomly selected 150 businesses—120 members (40 corporate members and 80 associate members) of the Multan Chamber of Commerce and Industry (MCCI), whose total membership in Multan was approximately 1,000 businesses at the time of the survey; and 30 businesses from the Women Chamber of Commerce and Industry Multan (WCCIM), whose total membership in Multan was approximately 140 businesses at the time of the survey. The assessment team conducted a third Phase I survey of all 103 participants of safe charity poster workshops conducted at Azm-e-Naujawan (AeN) community youth centers. The campaign expected another 850 community members to attend AeN safe charity poster exhibits. Through AeN center staff and poster workshop participants, the assessment team used a snowball approach to identify a sampling frame of approximately 400 visitors to the poster exhibitions. From this sampling frame, the assessment team selected a random sample of 121 exhibit visitors, stratified by gender. As with secondary farmers, the snowball approach to identifying secondary participants could not ensure activity participation or exposure to safe charity messaging, and may have been subject to a selection bias. The Phase II survey focused solely on farmer leaders and secondary farmers in Multan. During Phase II, the assessment team surveyed 124 farmer leaders, 112 of whom were surveyed in Phase I and 12 of whom were new respondents who replaced farmers that could not be reached or who were unable to participate. Similarly, the assessment team surveyed 152 secondary farmers, 131 of whom were also surveyed in Phase 1, and 21 of whom were new respondents who replaced farmers that could not be reached or who were unable to participate. Together, these surveys provide a comprehensive snapshot of how people in these communities give charity and the role that the risk of giving to violent extremist groups plays in charitable decision-making. The surveys captured three types of information. First, they probed how people give charity, including frequency of giving, type of giving, who in the household makes charitable giving decisions, why people give charity, and factors determining to whom people give charity. Second, the surveys probed people’s knowledge of the risk of giving to violent extremist groups, where people obtain information about safe charity, and how this knowledge affects decision-making. Third, the surveys probed participation in safe charity activities and the effect of this participation on knowledge and behaviors, including further dissemination of safe charity messaging. The survey data can be disaggregated by gender, age, income, religion, and respondent type, as well as period of charitable giving. The two phases of data collection provide important insights into how hyperlocal conditions of place and time affect charitable decision-making and knowledge and practice of safe charity. The survey team employed a longitudinal design, surveying the same farmers who participated in Phase I. By surveying the same respondents, the assessment team examined layered (or repeated) exposure to safe charity activities and compared perceptions around different types of giving. However, given the unique circumstances and distinct forms of charity common to each charitable giving period, differences in behavior between Phase I and II should not be construed as change in behavior attributable to the safe charity campaign. The surveys are supplemented by in-depth individual and group interviews with primary and secondary safe charity participants.

resource.name: Feed The Future Interim Population-Based Assessment of Cambodia, Module E1-06, Quantity of Food Consumed Produced at Home During the Last Week: Section 1
resource.description: This dataset records the amount of food consumed by the household that came from food produced at home during the 7 days before the survey from the first interim assessment of Feed the Future's population-based indicaors for the ZOI in Cambodia.  It has 1019 rows and 768 columns.   The ZOI is the Pursat, Battambang, Kampong Thom, and Siem Reap Provinces.  The sampling design called for a two-stage cluster sample.  In the first stage, 84 villages were selected; in the second stage, households were selected within each sampled village. The sampling of villages was stratified by province, with the number of villages in each stratum proportional to the population in the stratum and with villages selected with probability proportional to size, based on the 2013 Commune Database.  The data is split into survey modules.  Modules A through C includes location information, informed consent, and the household roster.  Module D includes household characteristics.  Module E is the expenditures module broken up into 8 different parts.  Modules F and G include the hunger scale data and WEIA index data.  Data in modules H and I include mother and child dietary diversity. In the process of migrating data to the current DDL platform, datasets with a large number of variables required splitting into multiple spreadsheets.  They should be reassembled by the user to understand the data fully.

resource.name: Program Evaluation of USAID/Uganda SUSTAIN Activity: USAID Staff Data
resource.description:
USAID/Uganda’s Strengthening Uganda’s Systems for Treating AIDS Nationally (SUSTAIN) activity supports Uganda’s Ministry of Health (MOH) to strengthen quality and comprehensive HIV/AIDS care, prevention, laboratory and tuberculosis (TB) services at selected regional referral and district health care facilities in Uganda, as well as build the capacity of the public health system to sustain these services. SUSTAIN is a six­-year USAID­-funded activity launched in 2010 and implemented by University Research Co., LLC (URC). SUSTAIN is one of many PEPFAR-­funded activities to address the HIV/AIDS epidemic in Uganda. The main objective of the SUSTAIN program evaluation was to examine the activity’s methodology for achieving its
objectives in order to inform future USAID design work. USAID noted that URC had performed well on SUSTAIN, as evidenced by its activity reports, but wanted an evaluation of the approach used by SUSTAIN to inform future program designs. SUSTAIN implementation adapted to contextual changes in the Government of Uganda's (GoU) HIV/AIDS strategy responding to a spike in new infections and people living with HIV, and major shifts in PEPFAR policy.

The dataset consists of recorded responses to a series of questions asked during key informant interviews (KII) or client focus groups regarding the delivery of HIV/AIDS related services. There are 11 spreadsheets, each recording the answers of a different set of actors in health service delivery: district health officers, focus groups comprised of clients (two spreadsheets), clinic staff, laboratory staff, implementing partners, lower level facility staff, Ministry of Health staff, regional referral hospital staff, SUSTAIN project staff, and USAID staff.

resource.name: FTF Ghana 2015 Interim Population-Based Survey: Women's Dietary Diversity
resource.description: Feed the Future (FTF) initiative in Ghana is a collaborative effort that supports country-owned processes and plans for improving food security and nutrition, particularly in the northern part of the country. These datasets cover the interim survey that took place in 2015 and was designed as a follow-up to the baseline survey that happened from 2012 to 2013. The survey covered a range of indicators organized around four groups: (1) economic well-being; (2) women and children anthropometry; (3) hunger and diet diversity; and (4) women's empowerment. The survey design involved two stages in which enumeration areas were selected followed by households. Data was collected in a face-to-face fashion using well-designed questionnaires and other study materials.

The full dataset file can be found as an attachment towards the bottom of the metadata.

Life of activity farmer data (collected through Form 6 between October 2014 and September 2017) for the Feed the Future Uganda Commodity Production and Marketing Activity. This data was collected from farmers who have been reached through CPM-related interventions and broadly speaking, captures changes in adoption of CPM-promoted practices and the resulting impacts on production (i.e. improved quality and increased quantities produced). Moreover, Form 6 data supports reporting for nine Feed the Future indicators. In addition to the datasets, supporting documents include Form 6 survey tools used for each survey and calculation guides for computing the nine Feed the Future indicators that Form 6 measures.

The data was originally stripped of most PII at time of submission, including demographicinformation of respondents (except the date of interview), GPS coordinates, and village information in some datasets. All of these PII have been removed as they provide no or limited usefulness to the data.

Agriculture is one of the most important components of the Ugandan economy, with 14 percent of gross domestic product, 85 percent of total export earning, and 73 percent of total employment. The Feed the Future intervention invested in increasing the production of maize, beans, and coffee through the appropriate use of high-quality agricultural inputs and decreasing the prevalence of counterfeit agricultural inputs, like mislabeled seeds or diluted fertilizers, in the market. It relied on an innovative market facilitation approach that empowers local actors such as the “Village Agent” to serve as role models in the agriculture industry and act as champions of best practices for theway agricultural inputs are bought and sold.

resource.name: Section I Changes in Dairy Production
resource.description: The survey interviewed 254 retailer shops in 10 sub-cities of Addis Ababa. 30 supermarkets, 20 mini-markets, 100 regular shops, 80 dairy shops and 24 open market shops selling dairy products were interviewed. Details of the sampling strategy is found in the attachment. The survey collected information on the characteristics of the shop, details of dairy products sold, prices and quality. Policy makers, research, and other stakeholders can use this data to analyses dairy value chain in Ethiopia and dairy retailing practices in Ethiopia. This data set was collected through research of the project “Improving the evidence and policies for better performing livestock systems in Ethiopia” lead by the International Food Policy Research Institution as part of the Feed the Future Innovation Lab for Livestock Systems.

A range of household level data elements were reported in all other datasets and should be removed from all datasets except household’s. Examples include dwelling characteristics (roof, floor, walls) and hunger scale questions.

We will use the following steps to anonymize the datasets:
1.	Use k-anonymity to mitigate the following variables: sex, dwelling characteristics, relationship to household head, type of toilets, education level, literacy level (read and write), district, urbanization. To achieve a threshold of k=3, we will recode some of these variables including dwelling characteristics, type of toilets, relationship to household head, education level, and literacy level  
2.	Aggregate age variable into 5 ages bands. 
3.	Apply a micro aggregation to children and women weights and heights. Micro Aggregation replaces each single value with local means calculated on batches of 3 records each. 
4.	Top code the age and estimated price of house. Any reported house age value above 100 years was recoded as 100; any estimated price at 5 000 000 or above was replaced with the mean price of houses costing 5 000 000 or more. 
5.	      5. Capping household size to 13. To achieve this, we will randomly select out of the datasets individual members from these large households who do not participate anywhere else in the survey other than their membership to household. Initially, the largest household had 21 members; after this process, this household would have 13 members. The median household in Kenya is about 4.4. In this data, the median remains at 5.0 before and after households disclosure risk mitigation.

resource.name: Feed The Future Interim Population-Based Assessment of Cambodia, Modules H-I, Anthropometry and Food Consumed by Children: Section 1
resource.description: This dataset records the anthropometry of the mothers and children as well as the food consumed by the children from the first interim assessment of Feed the Future's population-based indicaors for the ZOI in Cambodia.  It has 1,019 rows and 866 columns.  The ZOI is the Pursat, Battambang, Kampong Thom, and Siem Reap Provinces.  The sampling design called for a two-stage cluster sample.  In the first stage, 84 villages were selected; in the second stage, households were selected within each sampled village. The sampling of villages was stratified by province, with the number of villages in each stratum proportional to the population in the stratum and with villages selected with probability proportional to size, based on the 2013 Commune Database.  The data is split into survey modules.  Modules A through C includes location information, informed consent, and the household roster.  Module D includes household characteristics.  Module E is the expenditures module broken up into 8 different parts.  Modules F and G include the hunger scale data and WEIA index data.  Data in modules H and I include mother and child dietary diversity. In the process of migrating data to the current DDL platform, datasets with a large number of variables required splitting into multiple spreadsheets.  They should be reassembled by the user to understand the data fully.

resource.name: West Usambara Plateau Soil Properties and Classification Data
resource.description:
In this manuscript, we synthesize current and legacy data from multiple studies to better understand the distribution and diversity of soil types and their properties in the Plateau physiographic region of the West Usamabara Mountains in Northeastern Tanzania. Analysis of soil properties and soil classification in the resulting dataset of 468 sites by land use, landscape position, and elevation revealed important relationships relevant for management and land use planning. These sites occurred across a range of landscape positions and an elevation gradient from 1040 – 2240 m.a.s.l. Soil diversity at the U.S. Order and WRB Reference Group levels was higher than expected, with five U.S. soil orders and seven WRB Reference Groups described in the dataset, and the highest soil diversity occurring at lower landscape positions. We found that soil organic carbon (SOC) and pH were two master variables that were correlated most other soil properties. Sites under cultivated land uses had the lowest topsoil soil organic carbon (SOC) concentrations, and SOC generally increased with increasing elevation. Mature forest and charcoal production areas did not significantly differ in their depth distributions of SOC. Valley soils had significantly lower surface SOC concentrations but higher exchangeable bases and pH values than all other landscape positions. Soil pH decreased by an average of 3.5 units across the entire elevation gradient and decreased by 1 unit with elevation even after SOC, land use and landscape position were included in multiple regression models. Local pedotransfer functions were developed to assist with the use of pH, clay and SOC as proxies for more difficult to measure soil properties such as cation exchange capacity (CEC) and base saturation (B.S.), bulk density and total phosphorus. Phosphorus (P) and potassium (K) were
identified as the most likely limiting nutrients in West Usambaran plateau soils in general. This information is critical for sustainable land management which will be applicable to the soils of other mountain complexes in the Eastern Arc chain.

resource.description:
The purpose of this study is to evaluate the impact that the Feed the Future Nutrition-led Agriculture Project for Food Security in Senegal (known as "Yaajeende") has had on reducing malnutrition and poverty in its intervention area.

This report details the findings, conclusions and recommendations of a mixed-methods quasi-experimental final impact evaluation (FIE) of the United States Agency for International Development’s (USAID) $50 million, seven-year Feed the Future Nutrition-Led Agriculture Project for Food Security in Senegal, known as “Yaajeende.” The National Cooperative Business Association’s Cooperative League of the USA (NCBA CLUSA) implemented the project. To combat poverty and child malnutrition, Yaajeende sought to accelerate the participation of the very poor in rural economic growth and improve the four dimensions of food security: availability, access, utilization and stability. Yaajeende worked in 790 villages across 49 municipalities (“communes” in French) and nine departments in the Matam, Tambacounda, Kédougou and Kolda regions. The project’s implementation period was November 1, 2010, to September 30, 2017.

The FIE aims to provide USAID with an evidence base on the impacts of the nutrition-led agriculture (NLA) approach that the project utilized on its key objectives, including reduced poverty and malnutrition. The findings are expected to provide accountability and learning value to USAID, including both the Senegal Mission and USAID/Feed the Future. Additional stakeholders include the Government of Senegal, implementing partners and other agencies, donors and practitioners active in nutrition, health, agriculture and integrated sectors.

resource.name: Data on food consumption in Zinder and Maradi in Niger: Section 1
resource.description: This dataset describes the foods consumed by the household surveyed as part of Baseline Study of Food for Peace Title II Development Food Assistance Program in the Maradi and Zinder regions in Niger.  It has 3,200 columns and 6,861 rows.   In fiscal year 2012, USAID's Office of Food for Peace (FFP) awarded fuding to private voluntary organizations (PVOs) to design and implement a multi-year Title II development food assistance program in Niger. The main purpose of the Title II program is to improve long-term food security of chronically food insecure population in the target regions. FFP contracted a firm, ICF International to conduct a baseline study in targeted areas of the country prior to the start of the new program.  The purpose of the study was to assess the current status of key indicators, have a better understanding of prevailing conditions and perceptions of the population in the implementation areas, and serve as a point of comparison for future final evaluations.  Results would also be used to further refine program targeting and, where possible, to understand the relationship between variables to inform program design.  The study was conducted in 2013, while FFP expects to conduct final evaluations as close as possible to the end of the program five years later. In the process of migrating data to the current DDL platform, datasets with a large number of variables required splitting into multiple spreadsheets.  They should be reassembled by the user to understand the data fully.

resource.name: FTF Ghana 2015 Interim Population-Based Survey: Anthropometry for Children
resource.description: Feed the Future (FTF) initiative in Ghana is a collaborative effort that supports country-owned processes and plans for improving food security and nutrition, particularly in the northern part of the country. These datasets cover the interim survey that took place in 2015 and was designed as a follow-up to the baseline survey that happened from 2012 to 2013. The survey covered a range of indicators organized around four groups: (1) economic well-being; (2) women and children anthropometry; (3) hunger and diet diversity; and (4) women's empowerment. The survey design involved two stages in which enumeration areas were selected followed by households. Data was collected in a face-to-face fashion using well-designed questionnaires and other study materials.

resource.name: Agricultural Land Dynamics and Land Policy in Rural Tanzania 2016: Productive Assets Dataset
resource.description:
This dataset contains information about capital assets owned by the household and their value. The table can be combined with other datasets in this data asset using the 'hhid' column.

The purpose of collecting these data was to examine farm expansion and labor markets in rural Tanzania. Data were collected in 8 rural districts of Tanzania: Mvomero, Kilombero, Njombe, Kiteto, Magu, Moshi Rural, Mkuranga and Liwale.

The data were collected through the Feed the Future Innovation Lab for Food Security Policy (FSP).

resource.name: Health Policy Plus (HP+) Midterm Performance Evaluation Dataset
resource.description: This is a Midterm Performance Evaluation of the Health Policy Plus (HP+) Project. The purpose of the evaluation is to provide an independent assessment of HP+ progress toward achieving project goals and objectives. Evaluation questions focus on: a) the extent to which HP+ technical approaches have enabled achievement of project objectives and met indicators; b) the current level of satisfaction of USAID and other partners with project progress to date; and c) emerging trends and needs in health policy that might be addressed in this or future projects. Methods included review of background documents, review of a midterm self-assessment and other information provided by Palladium based on questions posed by the team, detailed interviews with knowledgeable informants, and an online e-survey. Findings and conclusions were that HP+ progress in achieving program results in its four main technical areas (policy, advocacy, health financing, and accountability/governance) is on track; demand for HP+ in health financing has increased rapidly, indicative both of growing need for this assistance and satisfaction with work completed so far; on the whole, stakeholders say they are very satisfied with results being achieved; there remain some challenges and areas for improvement going forward; and there are a number of important emerging policy needs that could be addressed in this or future projects.
